Why the dash-dot matters

It is not a texture choice. In technical drawing, a dash-dot line is the convention for a datum or centreline — the fixed reference an object is measured against. Your pace line is exactly that.

So the mark inherits a grammar rather than inventing one: solid means measured, dash-dot means reference, and the relationship between them is the reading. It also gives the whole identity a second usable device — dash-dot rules can mark projected or derived figures anywhere in the product, which is the ≈ problem from the provenance rule solved graphically.

Where I'd land: I, then G.

I is the one that stops being a chart. Cropping the pair full-bleed kills every cap and terminal, and the plate gives the brand a surface — something to print, emboss, stamp on a release. It needs one decision from you: hard square, or a plate with the corners softened to sit beside OS icons.

G is the most articulate and the most literal. H is the cleanest abstraction but drifts toward generic punctuation.

Say which, and whether the plate should be square or softened, and I'll build the chosen one out in full.
